objectives: To carry out the experiment as outlined in the laboratory manual.
apparatus: Voltmeter, 0 – 300/600 V AC, with selector switch (1)
Wattmeters, 5 A, 300 V (2), and two-way switch S1 (1)

Note: The one-wattmeter method works only when the load is balanced, because the same reading pattern is assumed in all three phases. The two-wattmeter method does not need the load to be balanced, but it is exact only when no current flows in the neutral wire. Throughout this experiment, all connections were checked by a supervisor before power was switched on.

theory.text:
A three-phase supply has three voltages of equal size that are 120° apart in time. In a star connection, one end of each of the three coils is joined at a common point called the neutral point (N), and the other ends are connected to the lines R (red), Y (yellow) and B (blue). The voltage between a line and the neutral is called the phase voltage (Vp), and the voltage between any two lines is called the line voltage (VL). The phase sequence used in this experiment is R-Y-B.

When the load is balanced, all three phases take the same current. In this case the line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage, the line current is equal to the phase current, and the three currents cancel each other at the star point, so the neutral wire carries no current:

VL = √3 × Vp IL = Ip IN = 0

The power taken by a three-phase load is the sum of the powers in its three phases. For a balanced load with power factor cos φ, this is P = 3 Vp Ip cos φ = √3 VL IL cos φ. For a purely resistive load, cos φ = 1. For an unbalanced load, the power of each phase must be found separately and added:

P = IR VRN + IY VYN + IB VBN

In the one-wattmeter method, the current coil of the wattmeter is placed in line R, and the pressure coil is joined to line R at one end and, through the switch S1, to line Y (position 1) or line B (position 2) at the other end. The two readings are W1 = VL IL cos (30° + φ) and W2 = VL IL cos (30° − φ). Their sum gives the total power:

W1 + W2 = √3 VL IL cos φ

In the two-wattmeter method, the current coils of two wattmeters are placed in two lines (R and Y here), and their pressure coils are joined to the third line (B), which is the common line. The total power is the algebraic sum of the two readings, P = W1 + W2. For a balanced load, the readings are W1 = VL IL cos (30° − φ) and W2 = VL IL cos (30° + φ), and the power factor can be found from tan φ = √3 (W1 − W2) / (W1 + W2). The method is exact for a three-wire system. If the neutral wire carries current, the sum of the two readings differs from the true power, because part of the power is then taken through the neutral path.

When the load is unbalanced, the three line currents no longer cancel. The difference flows back through the neutral wire, so IN = IR + IY + IB (phasor sum). Because the neutral wire holds the star point at the supply neutral, the three phase voltages stay almost equal even though the currents are different.

The multiplication factor of a wattmeter is found from: (voltage range × current range × power factor) / full-scale divisions. For the 300 V, 5 A, unity power factor wattmeter with 150 divisions, this is (300 × 5 × 1) / 150 = 10 W per division.

precautions: All connections were checked by a supervisor before the power supply was switched on, as required throughout this experiment.
The variac was set to zero before starting, and the voltage was raised gradually to 300 V.
The load was checked to be balanced and in the correct position before the load switches were closed.
The meter ranges were checked to make sure they were not exceeded at any stage, especially the 5 A ammeters and wattmeters.
Care was taken to connect the current and pressure coils of the wattmeters with the correct polarity, to avoid a backward reading.
All meters were read with the eye directly in front of the pointer to avoid parallax error.
All equipment was switched off immediately after each part of the experiment was completed.
content.conclusion: Results validated the theoretical relationships described above.
learnings: Applied theoretical principles to experimental measurement.
